events.text: Halfway through a pine pass, a rope comes up out of the needles and a dozen men with cudgels step onto the road. Their leader has a speech ready about tolls.

ok.log: The leader is the last one standing, and then he is not. The villagers at the foot of the pass bring you rice cakes.

fail.log: There were more of them than the pass let you see. You walk on lighter and bruised.

effects.log: The leader counts it twice and wishes you a pleasant journey. He seems to mean it.

ok.log: You are over the ridge before the rope is back in their hands.

fail.log: A cudgel catches your shoulder on the way past. You keep running anyway.

events.text: A whole mountain stronghold has come down to the road: fifty riders and a chief in a lacquered helmet who has heard of you, and wants to be the one who stopped you.

choices.text: Challenge the chief before his riders

ok.log: The chief yields on one knee. His riders scatter into the hills, and the road is safe for a season.

fail.log: He is better than his helmet. You cut your way out with nothing to show for it but the cuts.

ok.log: By the end of the evening the chief is pouring your tea and asking your advice about his son.

fail.log: The chief does not like the sound of your voice. You leave by the long road, at speed.

effects.log: Three days out of your way, but nobody bleeds for it.

events.text: By a stream an old hermit is trying to catch fish with his bare hands, and failing, cheerfully. He looks up at you as if you were late.

effects.log: He eats like a man who has not eaten in a week and talks like one who has not talked in a year. Somewhere in the talk is a thing about breathing you had never understood.

choices.text: Ask him to teach you something

effects.log: He makes you stand in the cold stream until sunset. You are not sure it was a lesson. Your next forms come easier.
When you look back he has caught one, and is holding it up for you to see.

events.text: A cloth merchant with three carts and no guards asks if you are going the same way. He has heard the road ahead is not what it was.

ok.log: Thieves come at dusk on the second day and leave faster than they came. The merchant pays double.

fail.log: You keep the carts, but not the merchant's best bolt of silk, or your temper. He pays half.

choices.text: Walk ahead and scout for him

ok.log: You find the ambush before it finds him. The carts go round it, and the merchant presses silver into your hand.

fail.log: You miss them, and so do they: the carts take another road by luck. The merchant pays you for the walk.

choices.text: Wish him luck and go on alone

effects.log: You hear later that he arrived. You do not hear how.

events.text: Behind a waterfall, where the cliff should be solid, the spray hangs in a dark square. Someone cut steps into the rock there, long ago, and then tried to hide them.

ok.log: A dry chamber, a cold stone bed, words carved on the wall in a hand nobody writes any more. You sit with them until the light goes. Further in, a sealed door. You mark the place.

fail.log: The wet steps throw you into the pool. You come up laughing, and soaked, and you mark the place for another day.

choices.text: Mark it on your map and go on

effects.log: You draw the falls, the cliff and the dark square, and fold the paper small.

choices.text: Leave it to whoever hid it

effects.log: Some doors are hidden for a reason. You walk on, and the falls close behind you.

events.text: A storm drives you into a roadside shrine. Another traveller is already there, wringing out a sleeve, and makes room for you by the little fire without a word.

choices.text: Share the fire and the talk

effects.log: You talk until the rain stops, and part without names. It is the best evening of the journey.
Thunder in the hills, rain on the roof, the fire ticking. Your breathing settles into all of it.
You arrive a day early and a week ill.

events.text: At an inn on the road a storyteller is telling a tale to a full room, and it takes you a long moment to understand that the tale is about you. Most of it is wrong.

effects.log: The room turns to look. Half of them believe you; the other half like his version better.

choices.text: Buy him a drink and say nothing

effects.log: He drinks it, thanks you, and adds a dragon to the third part. You let him.
You eat in your room. Through the floor you hear yourself win a duel you lost.

events.text: A small child is sitting at a crossroads, crying with great dignity, and will not say where home is until you sit down too.

effects.log: Home is a farm two hills away, and a mother who runs the last part of the road. Word of it goes round the villages.

choices.text: Give the child to the next carter

effects.log: The carter knows the family. You watch the cart out of sight.

choices.text: Point the way and go on

effects.log: The child goes the way you pointed. You hope it was the right one.

events.text: At the edge of a village a crowd is waiting for you on the road, and an old one at the front is holding something up for you to see: a broken name tablet from a family altar.

effects.log: They speak for an hour. You do not argue. Afterwards the road opens, and a few of them nod.
Silver is not what they wanted, but it is something. The crowd breaks up slowly.
Nobody quite dares to stop you. The stones start after you have passed.

events.text: Villagers recognise you at a ford and will not let you pass until you have eaten. An old man insists on carrying your pack across himself, and nearly drowns doing it.

effects.log: Rice, pickles, a bed under the eaves, and children who ask you to show them a form.

choices.text: Teach the children a form before you go

effects.log: They practise it in a row by the ford as you leave, all of them wrong, all of them proud.

choices.text: Thank them and go on quickly

effects.log: They wave you off with more food than you can carry.

events.text: Families with handcarts fill the road, walking away from the sects' war: grandmothers, chickens, a loom tied on with rope. Nobody looks back.

choices.text: Give them silver for the road (30 taels)

effects.log: A woman takes it without a word and puts it in her child's hand.

choices.text: Walk with them to the next town

effects.log: Nobody bothers a column with you in it. At the town gate they cheer you, a thin, tired cheer.
You go round them by the fields. It takes most of the day.

events.text: On the frozen river at the border, riders from across the steppe are driving off a village's horses. The villagers are watching from the bank with pitchforks and no hope.

choices.text: Go out onto the ice after them

ok.log: The horses come home, and so do you, frozen to the knees. The garrison captain buys you a bowl of hot tea.

fail.log: The ice and the raiders together are too much. You get back to the bank, which is something.

ok.log: Two riders go down and the rest let the horses go rather than wait for a third.

fail.log: Your arrows skitter across the ice. The riders laugh, and are gone.

choices.text: Help the village count what is left

effects.log: You stay two days and mend a fence. It is not much. They remember it.

events.text: A pedlar in Sichuan, in the Tang family's colours, offers you a little lacquered box of remedies: "For the bites, the fevers, and the friends who turn out not to be."

effects.log: Inside are seven tiny jars and a slip of instructions in very small writing. You read it twice.

choices.text: Ask what is really in the jars

ok.log: You name three of the herbs before the pedlar stops you, smiling. "Take one," she says, "for knowing."

fail.log: You sniff the wrong jar. You lose the afternoon, and most of your sense of smell, for a day.

effects.log: The pedlar bows. In Sichuan, a polite refusal is also a kind of remedy.

events.text: On a Jiangnan canal barge a young poet is stuck on the last line of a poem about the willows, and asks the whole deck for help.

ok.log: The deck goes quiet, then applauds. By the next town the poem has your line in it, and your name.

fail.log: The poet thanks you kindly and uses someone else's line. It is better. You admit it.

choices.text: Buy silk at the next landing

effects.log: A merchant on the barge sells you a bolt cheap, for the pleasure of the poem.
You do not help the poet, and you do not need to. The willows are enough.

events.text: At a harbour town on the coast the fishermen will not put out to sea: a pirate junk has been sitting at the mouth of the bay for a week, waiting for someone to try.

ok.log: The captain goes over the side. The junk is towed in by noon, and the town feasts on her stores.

fail.log: You end up in the bay, swimming for a fishing boat. The pirates sail off laughing, at least.

choices.text: Trade with the foreign ships instead

effects.log: A ship from beyond the sea sells you a little bottle of something that smells of another world. It sells on for twice the price.

choices.text: Wait for the pirates to leave

effects.log: They leave on the ninth day. The fishermen go out. Nobody sings about it.

events.text: A Silk Road caravan has lost its guide in a sandstorm and sits in a ring of camels at an oasis, arguing in four languages about which way the road went.

ok.log: Stars, a dry riverbed and the lie of the dunes. By morning the caravan is moving, and its master owes you.

fail.log: You find a road. It is not the road. You find the road two days later, and the camels forgive you first.

effects.log: A trader with a turquoise ring sells you a pouch of dried flowers that steady the breath.

choices.text: Rest at the oasis and go on

effects.log: Dates, cold water and shade. The caravan argues on behind you.

events.text: On the great road through the Central Plains, the disciples of a great sect have set up a table under a banner and are watching every traveller who passes, measuring.

ok.log: The examiner bows and writes your name in a book. "Should you ever want a gate," she says, "ours is open."

fail.log: The examiner is kind about it, which is worse. You walk on with your face hot.

choices.text: Ask them the news of the sects

effects.log: They know everything: who is at war, who has a new leader, whose disciples are leaving. You listen for an hour.
You feel their eyes on your back for the next half li.
